title: Lamentations 1:1–11
context: A narrator describes the city that sits solitary: she who was full of people has become as a widow, a princess among the provinces now a slave. The roads to Zion mourn; Judah has gone into captivity; the LORD has afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions; children have been led away; the sanctuary has been entered by nations. In 1:9 and 1:11 the WEB marks brief first-person appeals—“See, LORD, my affliction” and “Look, LORD, and see, for I have become despised”—as Zion’s own interjections inside the narrator’s report. The grief is to be read with pastoral care. Shame, hunger, and the ruined house are named as the poem names them, without sensational description. Wrath and grief are shared ground here, not a new contrast over a believer’s standing. 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52 tell of Jerusalem’s fall, and Deuteronomy 28 names covenant curses; those texts may be named by reference without being blended with this lament. The book does not name its author in these verses; a connection with Jeremiah is common and may be left hedged. Chapter 1 is often described as an alphabetic lament, with a verse for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. That form can be noted without listing the letters, and it is not required in order to hear the grief the verses speak.

verses.text: How the city sits solitary, that was full of people! She has become as a widow, who was great among the nations! She who was a princess among the provinces has become a slave!
verses.arminianNotes:
“How the city sits solitary, that was full of people!” The opening cry is over a city once full, now alone. She has become as a widow, who was great among the nations, and a princess among the provinces who has become a slave. The city is spoken of as a woman in grief; that personification should be heard as the poem’s way of naming a people’s loss, not as a cue for graphic comment.

Arminian readers take the “How” as a real lament over a real fall, a solitude and servitude the hearers are meant to feel with the city, not a riddle to be solved before mourning is allowed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a public cry over Jerusalem’s reversal: fullness to solitude, greatness to widowhood, a princess become a slave.

Shared ground: the verse is grief over the city’s fall. 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52 may be named later as the narrative of that fall, without being merged into this opening line.

verses.text: She weeps bitterly in the night. Her tears are on her cheeks. Among all her lovers she has no one to comfort her. All her friends have dealt treacherously with her. They have become her enemies.
verses.arminianNotes:
“She weeps bitterly in the night. Her tears are on her cheeks.” No one among her lovers comforts her; her friends have dealt treacherously and become her enemies. “lovers” and “friends” are often taken of former allies, or of false trusts; the verse does not define them, and that is held lightly. The point is abandonment in tears, and it is left in that sober sense.

Arminian readers hear a city truly forsaken in the night, her hoped-for comforters gone, a grief that does not need to be turned into a scheme before it can be heard.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same night weeping and the failure of lovers and friends as the poem’s account of isolation after the fall, with former supports now turned to enmity.

Shared ground: there is no comforter here. The identifications of the lovers may stay modest.

verses.text: Judah has gone into captivity because of affliction and because of great servitude. She dwells among the nations. She finds no rest. All her persecutors overtook her in her distress.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Judah has gone into captivity because of affliction and because of great servitude.” She dwells among the nations and finds no rest; her persecutors overtook her in her distress. The line names both captivity and the affliction and servitude that belong to it. Rest is not found in the places of exile this verse describes.

Arminian readers take the captivity as a real displacement of Judah, overtaken in distress, a loss to be mourned rather than explained away.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same going into captivity, the dwelling among the nations, and the lack of rest, as the poem’s account of Judah after the fall.

Shared ground: Judah is in exile and has no rest. The verse does not yet name the date of the deportation, and need not be forced into a single chronology with 2 Kings 25.

verses.text: The roads to Zion mourn, because no one comes to the solemn assembly. All her gates are desolate. Her priests sigh. Her virgins are afflicted, and she herself is in bitterness.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The roads to Zion mourn, because no one comes to the solemn assembly.” Gates are desolate; priests sigh; the city’s young women are afflicted; she herself is in bitterness. The empty roads and the silenced assembly are the public face of the loss, including the loss of worship.

Arminian readers hear a real end of pilgrimage and feast, a bitterness in the city and among those who served her worship, to be read with care and without turning the afflicted young women into a scene.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the mourning roads, desolate gates, sighing priests, and bitterness as the poem’s picture of Zion without her assembly.

Shared ground: the solemn assembly has ceased. The grief includes the ruined pattern of worship, and it is shared, not a party contrast.

verses.text: Her adversaries have become the head. Her enemies prosper; for the LORD has afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions. Her young children have gone into captivity before the adversary.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Her adversaries have become the head. Her enemies prosper; for the LORD has afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions.” The poem does not hide either the enemies’ rise or the LORD’s afflicting, and it names the multitude of transgressions as the reason. “Her young children have gone into captivity before the adversary.” That last clause should be stated as the verse states it, soberly, without added description. How God relates to the adversaries who have become the head may be compared with the existing box at Judges 9:23, without restating that discussion.

Arminian readers hear both a real guilt and a real grief: the LORD has afflicted her for transgressions, and children have been led away, a loss named here with restraint.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hold together the enemies’ prospering, the LORD’s afflicting, and the named transgressions, with the children gone into captivity before the adversary.

Shared ground: wrath and guilt and this grief belong in one verse. The traditions need not divide here over whether the lament is allowed to tell all three.

verses.text: All majesty has departed from the daughter of Zion. Her princes have become like deer that find no pasture. They have gone without strength before the pursuer.
verses.arminianNotes:
“All majesty has departed from the daughter of Zion.” Her princes are like deer that find no pasture, gone without strength before the pursuer. The majesty is gone; the leaders flee exhausted. The “daughter of Zion” is the city and people so named, not a separate character to be pressed.

Arminian readers take the departed majesty and the failing princes as a public undoing, a people whose strength is spent, which the lament is right to name.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same departure of majesty and the princes’ weakness before the pursuer, the daughter of Zion stripped of the dignity the opening verses remembered.

Shared ground: leadership and glory have failed together. There is no party contrast over the image of the deer.

verses.text: Jerusalem remembers in the days of her affliction and of her miseries all her pleasant things that were from the days of old; when her people fell into the hand of the adversary, and no one helped her. The adversaries saw her. They mocked at her desolations.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Jerusalem remembers in the days of her affliction and of her miseries all her pleasant things that were from the days of old;” In the present misery she remembers former pleasant things; when her people fell, no one helped, and the adversaries mocked at her desolations. Memory itself has become part of the pain.

Arminian readers hear a real remembering in affliction, a contrast between old pleasant things and present mockery, which deepens the grief rather than relieving it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same memory as the poem’s: in affliction Jerusalem remembers the days of old, and the adversaries mock her desolations when no one helped her.

Shared ground: memory and mockery stand together here. The “days of old” are not dated in the verse and is not turned into a reconstructed history.

verses.text: Jerusalem has grievously sinned. Therefore she has become unclean. All who honored her despise her, because they have seen her nakedness. Yes, she sighs and turns backward.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Jerusalem has grievously sinned. Therefore she has become unclean.” Those who honored her despise her, “because they have seen her nakedness.” She sighs and turns backward. The sin is named first, and the shame follows. The language of uncleanness and nakedness is the poem’s way of speaking of public disgrace; it is left in that sober sense, without graphic description or lingering detail.

Arminian readers take the grievous sin as a real confession the narrator makes for the city, and the resulting shame as a grief to be handled with care, not as a scene to be expanded.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same order: grievous sin, then uncleanness and being despised, with the shame named only as the poem names it.

Shared ground: Jerusalem has sinned, and she is disgraced. The verse is a lament over that truth, not an invitation to sensational reading.

verses.text: Her filthiness was in her skirts. She didn’t remember her latter end. Therefore she has come down astoundingly. She has no comforter. “See, LORD, my affliction; for the enemy has magnified himself.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Her filthiness was in her skirts. She didn’t remember her latter end.” She has come down astoundingly and has no comforter. Then Zion’s own voice breaks in, as the WEB marks it: “See, LORD, my affliction; for the enemy has magnified himself.” The first sentences stay with the narrator’s sober charge; the quoted appeal is Zion’s cry to the LORD. The image of filthiness should be treated as the poem’s language of defilement and forgotten end, without elaboration.

Arminian readers hear both the charge and the prayer: a fall she did not remember in time, and a first-person plea that the LORD would see her affliction, a cry the city itself is now made to speak.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same turn: the narrator’s word about a forgotten latter end, then Zion’s appeal, “See, LORD, my affliction;” when the enemy has magnified himself.

Shared ground: there is no comforter, and the city asks the LORD to see. The interjection is to be named as Zion’s, not absorbed as if the narrator were still the only voice.

verses.text: The adversary has spread out his hand on all her pleasant things; for she has seen that the nations have entered into her sanctuary, concerning whom you commanded that they should not enter into your assembly.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The adversary has spread out his hand on all her pleasant things; for she has seen that the nations have entered into her sanctuary, concerning whom you commanded that they should not enter into your assembly.” The loss now includes the sanctuary itself, entered by nations who were not to enter the assembly. The “you” appears to address the LORD; that shift can be noted without forcing a full change of speaker before the next verse’s quoted cry. The ruined house should be spoken of with care, as a holiness violated, not as a scene to be enlarged.

Arminian readers hear a real trespass against what God had commanded about the assembly, a grief over the sanctuary that belongs with the city’s other losses, and that 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 52 also know in narrative form, without those accounts being merged here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same entry of the nations into the sanctuary as the poem’s central wound in this verse, against the command that they should not enter the assembly.

Shared ground: the holy place has been entered. The traditions share the grief, and need not divide over the addressee of the “you.”

verses.text: All her people sigh. They seek bread. They have given their pleasant things for food to refresh their soul. “Look, LORD, and see, for I have become despised.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“All her people sigh. They seek bread. They have given their pleasant things for food to refresh their soul.” Hunger is named plainly: people sigh, seek bread, and trade what was pleasant for food. The report is kept brief and sober. Then Zion speaks again: “Look, LORD, and see, for I have become despised.” The first-person appeal matches the cry in verse 9 and prepares the longer speech that follows from verse 12.

Arminian readers hear a people reduced to seeking bread, and a city that asks the LORD to look at her despised state, a prayer that does not deny the hunger and does not turn it into a lesson beyond the lament.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same sighing, the search for bread, and the giving of pleasant things for food, then Zion’s “Look, LORD, and see,”

Shared ground: famine and shame are both before the LORD in this verse. The verse is left as the poem gives it, without added detail or an application lecture.
